p:
When people are asked to make a choice, economists traditionally assumed that the way the options are presented should not matter. A rational person, the argument went, weighs costs and benefits and picks whatever serves her best, regardless of which box happens to be ticked in advance. A large body of research now suggests otherwise. In many settings, the option that takes effect when a person does nothing, known as the default, exerts a remarkable pull on behavior.

When the same firms enroll workers automatically and let them leave if they wish, participation often rises sharply. p:
Before the middle of the nineteenth century, most towns kept their own time. Noon was the moment the sun stood highest over the local church or town hall, and because the sun moves westward, a town a few dozen kilometers to the east reached noon a little earlier than its neighbor. For centuries this caused little trouble. Travel was slow, and a gap of several minutes between places hardly mattered to someone who needed a whole day to cover the distance between them.
The railway changed this. Trains made it possible to cross a region in hours, and timetables had to tell passengers when a train would leave one station and reach another. If each station followed its own local time, a single schedule might refer to dozens of slightly different clocks, and the risk of confusion, and even of collision on single-track lines, grew. Railway companies therefore began to adopt one standard time across their networks, usually that of a major city. Over the following decades, governments turned this practice into law, and the world was eventually divided into time zones.
The change was not welcomed everywhere. In some places residents complained that an abstract time set by distant authorities had replaced the natural rhythm of the sun. A few towns kept two clocks on public buildings, one showing local time and the other railway time, as if unwilling to choose between them.
Historians have argued that standard time did more than make travel efficient. It encouraged people to coordinate their lives with strangers far away, and it turned punctuality, measured to the minute, into a widely shared value. In this sense, the clock on the station wall helped to shape a new kind of social discipline, one that factories and schools would later reinforce.

t: 出版バイアス：20チームの例
p:
Scientific journals have long preferred to publish studies that report striking, positive results. A paper showing that a new drug works, or that some habit predicts success, is more likely to attract readers than one concluding that nothing of interest was found. This preference seems harmless, but it can distort the picture of the world that the published record presents.
Imagine that twenty research teams test whether a certain food improves memory, and that in reality it has no effect. By chance alone, one or two of these teams may obtain results that appear significant. If only those studies are published while the others stay in desk drawers, readers will conclude that the evidence for the effect is consistent, when in fact it is nothing of the kind. Researchers call this the "file drawer problem."
The difficulty is made worse by the pressures on scientists themselves. Careers depend on publications, and publications depend on findings that editors find exciting. Under such conditions, researchers may be tempted, often with no intention to deceive, to try several ways of analyzing their data and report only the one that yields a clear result.
In recent years, a number of reforms have been proposed. One is preregistration, in which researchers state their hypotheses and methods before collecting data, so that later changes become visible. Another is the "registered report," which a journal agrees to publish on the basis of its design rather than its outcome. Supporters argue that such measures reward careful questions rather than lucky answers. Skeptics note that not all research can be planned in advance, and that exploratory work, which often leads to unexpected discoveries, should not be viewed with suspicion simply because its path was not mapped beforehand.

t: 贈与：関係が強まる理由
p:
In many societies, a gift is never simply a gift. Anthropologists who studied exchange in small communities observed that offering something to another person created an expectation that something would eventually be returned. To refuse a gift could be taken as an insult, and to accept one without ever giving back could leave a person in a position of lasting inferiority. Gifts, in other words, built and maintained relationships precisely because they placed people in each other's debt.
At first sight, modern market exchange seems to work on the opposite principle. When I buy bread from a shop, I pay the agreed price, and the deal is complete. Neither the baker nor I owe each other anything further, and we may never meet again. The very purpose of money, one might say, is to settle accounts so fully that no relationship needs to remain.
Yet the contrast can be overstated. Even in highly commercial societies, people take great care over the gifts they give to friends and relatives. Giving cash to a close friend on her birthday is often thought awkward, while a carefully chosen object, though it may cost the same, is welcomed. This suggests that what matters is not the value transferred but the attention and knowledge that the choice reveals. Similarly, people who return a favor too quickly, as if eager to be free of the obligation, may be thought cold.
Some scholars therefore argue that the two forms of exchange coexist within every society, each governing a different sphere of life. Markets allow strangers to trade efficiently without trust, while gifts sustain the ties of intimacy that markets cannot create. Problems arise, they suggest, when the logic of one sphere invades the other, as when friendship is measured in money.

Gifts allowed people to settle their accounts completely.
Gifts were always of equal value, so no one felt inferior.
Gifts could be refused without causing any offense.

At first sight, modern market exchange seems to work on the opposite principle. When I buy bread from a shop, I pay the agreed price, and the deal is complete. Neither the baker nor I owe each other anything further, and we may never meet again. The very purpose of money, one might say, is to settle accounts so fully that no relationship needs to remain.
Yet the contrast can be overstated. Even in highly commercial societies, people take great care over the gifts they give to friends and relatives. Giving cash to a close friend on her birthday is often thought awkward, while a carefully chosen object, though it may cost the same, is welcomed. This suggests that what matters is not the value transferred but the attention and knowledge that the choice reveals. Similarly, people who return a favor too quickly, as if eager to be free of the obligation, may be thought cold.
Some scholars therefore argue that the two forms of exchange coexist within every society, each governing a different sphere of life. Markets allow strangers to trade efficiently without trust, while gifts sustain the ties of intimacy that markets cannot create. Problems arise, they suggest, when the logic of one sphere invades the other, as when friendship is measured in money.

p:
Most of us assume that memory works like a recording. We experience an event, store a copy of it somewhere in the brain, and later play it back more or less faithfully. Decades of psychological research have made this picture hard to ( A ). Remembering, it turns out, is less like replaying a video than like rebuilding a scene from scattered pieces, with gaps filled in by expectation and later information.
In one well-known type of experiment, people watch a short film of a traffic accident and are then asked questions about it. When the question uses a more violent verb, asking how fast the cars were going when they "smashed" rather than "hit" each other, people give higher estimates of speed. Some even report seeing broken glass that was never in the film. The wording of a single question, in other words, can [alter] what people believe they saw.
Such findings carry serious implications for the courtroom. Eyewitness testimony is often highly persuasive to juries, especially when a witness speaks with confidence. Yet confidence and accuracy are only loosely related, and a witness's certainty may grow over time as the story is retold, even as the memory itself becomes less reliable. Several cases in which convicted people were later cleared by new evidence had relied heavily on witnesses who were ( B ) but mistaken.
It would be wrong, however, to conclude that memory is simply defective. A system that rebuilds rather than records has advantages. It allows us to draw general lessons from particular experiences, to combine fragments into new ideas, and to imagine the future by rearranging pieces of the past. The flexibility that makes memory unreliable as a witness may be the very feature that makes it useful as a guide to action.

p:
Every wave of technological change has been accompanied by fears that machines will leave large numbers of people without work. In the early nineteenth century, textile workers in England smashed the machines they believed were destroying their livelihoods. Similar fears returned with the computer. Today, advances in artificial intelligence have ( A ) the debate once more.
Looking back, economists generally conclude that the most dramatic predictions did not come true. Although particular jobs vanished, new ones emerged. Rising productivity lowered prices, which left consumers with more money to spend on other goods and services, and that spending in turn created demand for workers elsewhere.
This reassuring story, however, [glosses over] an important point. The fact that employment recovered in the long run says little about the people who lost their jobs in the short run. A weaver in his fifties could not easily become a railway engineer, and many displaced workers never regained their former income. The gains from technology were real, but they were unevenly shared, across groups and generations.
Some researchers argue that the present wave may differ from earlier ones in a crucial respect. Earlier machines mainly replaced physical labor or routine calculation, leaving tasks that required judgment, language and social skill to human beings. Newer systems are beginning to perform some of these tasks as well. If so, the range of work in which humans keep a clear advantage may shrink faster than before. ( B ), others caution that such predictions have been made before, and that the capacity of economies to invent new kinds of work has often been underestimated. Both sides agree that the pace of adjustment, and who bears its costs, will depend heavily on public policy.

p:
Democratic politics is usually imagined as a contest. Parties compete for votes and seats, interest groups lobby for advantage, and elections decide which side wins. Critics have long complained that this model rewards slogans more than reasoning, and that voters are rarely asked to consider the arguments of those they disagree with. In response, a number of countries and cities have experimented with an alternative: the citizens' assembly.
A citizens' assembly brings together a group of ordinary people, chosen at random but balanced to reflect the population by age, gender, region and other traits. Over several weekends, members hear from experts and advocates on a disputed issue, discuss the evidence in small groups, and finally make recommendations. Because members are not seeking reelection, they are free to change their minds, and observers often report that they do.
Supporters claim that such bodies can break deadlocks that elected politicians are unable or unwilling to resolve. When a proposal comes from people much like themselves who have studied the question carefully, voters may find it more ( A ) than one produced by professional politicians. Several assemblies have tackled divisive social issues and produced proposals that voters later approved.
Skeptics raise practical and principled objections. Randomly selected members, they note, have no mandate from the electorate and cannot be held [accountable] at the next election. The results also depend heavily on how the agenda is framed and which experts are invited, which gives considerable influence to the organizers. For these reasons, most proposals treat assemblies not as a ( B ) for elected legislatures but as a supplement to them, offering advice that politicians or voters remain free to accept or reject.

A citizens' assembly brings together a group of ordinary people, chosen at random but balanced to reflect the population by age, gender, region and other traits. Over several weekends, members hear from experts and advocates on a disputed issue, discuss the evidence in small groups, and finally make recommendations. Because members are not seeking reelection, they are free to change their minds, and observers often report that they do.
Supporters claim that such bodies can break deadlocks that elected politicians are unable or unwilling to resolve. When a proposal comes from people much like themselves who have studied the question carefully, voters may find it more ( A ) than one produced by professional politicians. Several assemblies have tackled divisive social issues and produced proposals that voters later approved.
Skeptics raise practical and principled objections. Randomly selected members, they note, have no mandate from the electorate and cannot be held [accountable] at the next election. The results also depend heavily on how the agenda is framed and which experts are invited, which gives considerable influence to the organizers. For these reasons, most proposals treat assemblies not as a ( B ) for elected legislatures but as a supplement to them, offering advice that politicians or voters remain free to accept or reject.
q: 次の英文を読み、空所（ B ）に入れるのに最も適当なものを選びなさい。

m: substitute for A＝Aの代わり／supplement to A＝Aの補足

f: 長文読解（語句・空所・言い換え）
p:
When antibiotics came into wide use in the 1940s, they transformed medicine. Infections that had routinely killed patients became easy to treat, and operations that had been too dangerous to attempt became common. Yet even some of the scientists who developed these drugs warned that bacteria might learn to ( A ) them, and that warning has proved accurate.
Resistance arises through natural selection. In any large population of bacteria, a few individuals may carry genetic changes that allow them to survive a particular drug. When the drug is applied, the others die, while the resistant ones survive and multiply until they dominate the population. Bacteria can also pass resistance genes to one another, even across species, which lets resistance spread far faster than it would through inheritance alone.
Human behavior has sped up this process. Antibiotics are often prescribed for illnesses caused by viruses, such as the common cold, against which they are useless. In many countries, large quantities of antibiotics are given to farm animals, not to cure disease but to promote growth, creating ideal conditions for resistant strains to emerge.
The problem is made worse by economics. Developing a new antibiotic is expensive, and because doctors are rightly urged to save new drugs for cases in which older ones fail, sales of a successful new antibiotic are likely to be modest. Drug companies therefore have little [incentive] to invest in the field, and few new classes of antibiotics have reached the market in recent decades. Some experts have proposed that governments pay companies a fixed reward for developing useful antibiotics, ( B ) of how many doses are eventually sold, so that the goal of protecting new drugs no longer conflicts with the goal of making a profit.
q: 次の英文を読み、空所（ A ）に入れるのに最も適当なものを選びなさい。
e: 科学者たちが警告したのは、細菌がやがて抗生物質に「耐える」ようになるかもしれないということで、それが正しかったとわかったと述べています。第2段落の「耐性は自然選択によって生じる」という説明にもつながるので、withstand（耐える・持ちこたえる）が正解です。細菌が抗生物質を produce（作る）、detect（検出する）、imitate（まねる）では、耐性の話につながりません。
m: withstand＝resist＝耐える

f: 長文読解（語句・空所・言い換え）
p:
It is natural to assume that native speakers of English hold an advantage in international communication. They can express subtle ideas without searching for words. Yet researchers who study conversations among speakers from many countries have reported a surprising pattern: native speakers are sometimes the hardest participants to understand.
The reason lies partly in habits that native speakers rarely notice. They tend to speak quickly, to use idioms drawn from local culture, and to make jokes whose meaning depends on shared background. Non-native speakers, by contrast, often develop a simpler, more explicit style when talking with one another. They check whether they have been understood, rephrase difficult points, and avoid expressions that might be [opaque] to listeners from other regions. As a result, a meeting among people who all learned English as a second language may run more smoothly than one that includes a single native speaker.
This finding challenges the view that the goal of language learning is to sound as much like a native speaker as possible. If English is used mainly as a common tool among people with different first languages, then the measure of success may be ( A ) rather than accuracy in imitating any one national variety. A learner who speaks with a clear accent but adapts readily to different listeners may communicate better than one who has mastered every local idiom.
None of this means that standards no longer matter. Grammar that departs too far from shared norms can still cause misunderstanding, and learners preparing for certain careers may need a specific variety. ( B ), the research suggests that native speakers themselves may need to learn something: how to adjust their language for listeners who do not share their assumptions.
q: 次の英文を読み、下線部［opaque］の意味として最も適当なものを選びなさい。
e: opaque はもともと「不透明な」ですが、ここでは表現について「意味がわかりにくい」の意味です。非母語話者どうしは、理解されたかを確かめ、難しい点を言い換え、他の地域の聞き手には〜かもしれない表現を避ける、という流れで、前の段落の「母語話者は地域文化の慣用句を使う」とも対応しています。「不快にさせる」「なじみがある」「堅すぎる」では、理解しやすさを論じる段落に合いません。
m: opaque⇔transparent（わかりやすい）

t: 誤り指摘：a number of の一致
q:
次の英文の［ ］で示した部分のうち、誤りを含むものを一つ選びなさい。
A number of [critical] questions [remains] unanswered, [despite] the [considerable] effort the researchers have made.

q:
次の英文の［ ］で示した部分のうち、誤りを含むものを一つ選びなさい。
Having been raised [in] a bilingual household, [it was] easy for her [to switch] between the two languages [without] hesitation.
e: 分詞構文の意味上の主語は、原則として主節の主語と一致しなければなりません。「バイリンガルの家庭で育てられた」のは彼女なので、主節の主語を she にして she found it easy to switch ～ とする必要があります。it was のままでは it が育てられたことになってしまいます（懸垂分詞）。raised in a household（家庭で育つ）の in、easy for her to switch の不定詞、without hesitation（ためらわずに）はいずれも正しい表現です。
m: 分詞構文の主語＝主節の主語

q:
次の英文の空所に入れるのに最も適当なものを選びなさい。
( ) the support of his colleagues, the project would have failed long before its completion.
e: 主節が would have failed（仮定法過去完了）なので、「もし〜がなかったら」という条件を表す Without が入ります（But for や If it had not been for と同じ意味）。With では「支援があったら失敗しただろう」となり意味が逆になります。Unless は接続詞なので、後ろに名詞だけでなく節が必要です。Except は「〜を除いて」で、条件の意味になりません。
m: Without A＝But for A＝If it had not been for A

q:
次の英文の空所に入れるのに最も適当なものを選びなさい。
The opposition party demanded that the full report ( ) published before the vote.
e: demand, insist, require, suggest など要求・提案を表す動詞の後の that 節では、動詞の原形（仮定法現在）か should＋原形を使います。主語が the full report で「公表される」という受動の意味なので be published が正解です。that 節には主語に対応する述語動詞が必要なので、分詞の being や不定詞の to be は入りません。has been は直説法の現在完了で、過去の要求の内容を表す that 節には使いません。
m: 要求・提案の that 節＝(should)＋原形

q:
次の英文の空所に入れるのに最も適当なものを選びなさい。
The village is ( ) that it does not appear on most maps of the region.
e: 「とても小さいので〜」は so＋形容詞＋that 節で表します。such は名詞を含む句と組むので、such a small village that ～ なら可能ですが、such small だけでは不可です。too ～ は that 節ではなく to 不定詞と組み（too small to appear ～）、very small that という形もありません。
m: so＋形容詞＋that／such (a)＋形容詞＋名詞＋that

t: 仮定法：倒置 Had S p.p.
q:
次の英文の空所に入れるのに最も適当なものを選びなさい。
Had the government acted sooner, the economic crisis ( ) avoided.
e: 文頭の Had the government acted は If the government had acted の if を省略した倒置で、過去の事実に反する仮定（仮定法過去完了）です。主節は助動詞の過去形＋have p.p. になるので could have been avoided が正解です。could be は現在の推量になり、時制が合いません。can have been は「〜したはずがある」という推量で、仮定法の主節には使いません。had been を入れると主節の形として成り立ちません。
m: Had S p.p., S would/could have p.p.

q:
次の英文の空所に入れるのに最も適当なものを選びなさい。
The theory, ( ) he devoted the last decade of his life, was finally accepted by the scientific community.
e: devote A to B（AをBにささげる）の B が先行詞 the theory にあたるので、前置詞 to を関係代名詞の前に置いた to which が正解です。which だけでは to が不足します。that は前置詞の直後に置けず、カンマの後の非制限用法にも使えません。what は先行詞を含む関係代名詞なので、the theory という先行詞があるこの文には使えません。
m: devote A to B → to which

q:
次の英文の空所に入れるのに最も適当なものを選びなさい。
The minister's remarks were deliberately ( ), allowing supporters and critics alike to read into them whatever they wished.
e: 支持者も批判者も「好きな意味を読み取れる」ようにした、という後半から、発言はわざと「あいまいな」ものだったとわかります。ambiguous が正解です。explicit（明確な）や candid（率直な）だと、解釈の余地がなくなるので後半と矛盾します。concise（簡潔な）は短さを表す語で、多様に解釈できることの説明にはなりません。
m: ambiguous＝2通り以上に解釈できる

q:
次の英文の空所に入れるのに最も適当なものを選びなさい。
The newly discovered documents ( ) doubt on the long-accepted account of the treaty's origins.
e: cast doubt on A で「Aに疑いを投げかける」というコロケーション（決まった語の組み合わせ）です。cast は過去形も cast なので、ここでは過去の意味で使われています。made、took、gave は doubt on とは結びつきません。ほかにも throw doubt on、raise doubts about などの言い方があります。
m: cast doubt on＝～に疑問を投げかける

次の英文の下線部［ ］に最も意味が近いものを選びなさい。
Her argument sounds attractive, but it does not [hold water] once you examine the statistics.
e: hold water は「（理論・議論が）筋が通る・正しいと認められる」という意味のイディオムで、主に否定文で使います。統計を調べると議論が成り立たない、という文意なので「論理的に説得力を保つ」が正解です。水を入れても漏れない器のように、穴のない議論というイメージです。感情に訴える、注目を集める、形式に従う、はいずれも意味が違います。
m: not hold water＝穴があって成り立たない

次の英文の空所に入れるのに最も適当なものを選びなさい。
Analysts ( ) the sharp rise in food prices to the poor harvest of the previous year.
e: attribute A to B で「AをBのせいにする・Aの原因をBに帰する」です。価格の高騰の原因を不作に帰した、という意味になります。contribute A to B は「AをBに寄付・貢献する」、distribute A to B は「AをBに配る」で文意に合いません。account は account for A（Aを説明する）の形で使い、account A to B という形はありません。
m: attribute A to B＝AをBのせいにする

q:
次の英文の空所に入れるのに最も適当なものを選びなさい。
In the ( ) of reliable evidence, the court had no choice but to dismiss the case.
e: in the absence of A で「Aがないので・Aがない場合に」という決まった表現です。信頼できる証拠がないので裁判所は訴えを退けるしかなかった、という意味になります。vacancy（空席・空室）、emptiness（空っぽであること）、omission（省略・脱落）はいずれも「〜がない」に通じる語ですが、in the ～ of の形で「〜がないので」という意味にはなりません。lack を使うなら for lack of A という形になります。
m: in the absence of＝～がないので

q:
次の英文の下線部［ ］に最も意味が近いものを選びなさい。
Facing strong opposition, the committee decided to [shelve] the redevelopment plan for the time being.
e: shelve は「棚に置く」から転じて「（計画などを）棚上げする・先送りする」の意味です。for the time being（当分の間）という語句とも合い、「検討を延期する」が正解です。put into practice（実行する）は逆の意味です。reject permanently（永久に却下する）は、一時的な保留という shelve の意味とずれます。announce publicly（公表する）も違います。
m: shelve＝put off＝棚上げ

q:
次の英文の空所に入れるのに最も適当なものを選びなさい。
Her contribution to the project was ( ); without it, nothing of value would have been achieved.
e: 後半の「それがなければ価値あることは何も達成されなかっただろう」から、貢献は「不可欠な」ものだったとわかります。indispensable が正解です。negligible（無視できるほど小さい）、superficial（表面的な）、redundant（余分な）はいずれも貢献を低く評価する語で、後半と矛盾します。
m: indispensable＝essential＝なくてはならない

q:
次の英文の空所に入れるのに最も適当なものを選びなさい。
The series of scandals seriously ( ) public trust in the government.
e: undermine は「（信頼・権威などを）徐々に損なう・むしばむ」で、trust を目的語にとるのに最も適しています。一連のスキャンダルが政府への信頼を大きく損なった、という意味です。underwent（undergo：経験する・受ける）、understated（understate：控えめに言う）、undertook（undertake：引き受ける）は、いずれも under- で始まる紛らわしい語ですが、文意に合いません。
m: undermine＝徐々に弱める

q:
次の英文の下線部［ ］に最も意味が近いものを選びなさい。
It took him several years to [come to terms with] the failure of his first company.
e: come to terms with A は「A（つらい現実など）を受け入れる・Aと折り合いをつける」という意味のイディオムです。最初の会社の失敗を受け入れるのに数年かかった、という意味なので accept が最も近い意味です。forget（忘れる）は受け入れるのとは違い、explain（説明する）や repeat（繰り返す）も意味が違います。
m: come to terms with＝受け入れる・折り合う

q:
次の英文の空所に入れるのに最も適当なものを選びなさい。
The professor's lecture was so ( ) that even specialists in the field struggled to follow it.
e: so ～ that 構文で「専門家でさえついていくのに苦労した」と続くので、講義は「難解な」ものだったはずです。abstruse（難解な）が正解です。lucid（明快な）は逆の意味です。trivial（ささいな）や brief（短い）では、専門家が苦労する理由になりません。abstruse は難度の高い語なので、obscure（わかりにくい）とあわせて覚えておきましょう。
m: abstruse⇔lucid（明快な）

Why did you reject it so quickly?

t: 図書館での会話：状況の説明
p:
Student: Excuse me. I'm looking for a book that's listed in the catalog, but it isn't on the shelf.
Librarian: Let me check. It says here that it was returned yesterday afternoon, so ( 1 )
Student: I see. Could you let me know when it's available? I need it for a paper due on Friday.
Librarian: Certainly. But ( 2 ) There's an electronic version you can read on the library website.
Student: Oh, that's even better. Thank you so much.
q: 次の会話文を読み、空所（1）に入れるのに最も適当なものを選びなさい。
c: it may not have been put back on the shelf yet.
it has been missing for several months.
you'll have to wait until next year.
you must have borrowed it yourself.
e: 司書は「昨日の午後に返却された」と確認し、so（だから）で結論を続けています。返却されたばかりなので「まだ棚に戻されていないのかもしれない」が自然です。may not have p.p. は「〜していないかもしれない」という過去の推量です。「数か月行方不明」は昨日返却されたことと矛盾します。「来年まで待つ」は理由がつながらず、「あなた自身が借りたに違いない」も根拠がありません。
m: may not have p.p.＝～しなかったかもしれない
